title: The Corpus Christi hymns (1264)
hookLine: the pope asks Thomas to write the texts for the new feast
last: WHAT IT IS, NOT HOW IT LOOKS.

cards: Pages of careful argument: substance, accidents, a change that moves nothing. Then the same man is handed a different job.
Tradition says Pope Urban the Fourth, setting up a new feast for the Body of Christ, asked Thomas Aquinas to write its texts: the prayers, the antiphons, the hymns to be sung.
So the professor who wrote the Summa sits down to write songs. And the songs he's credited with are still sung at Benediction, at processions, on Holy Thursday night.
Today: what happens when a theologian has to make it rhyme.

teach.h: SING, MY TONGUE: AN OLD OPENING.
teach.b: Start with the first line of the Pange lingua: "Pange, lingua, gloriosi Corporis mysterium." Sing, my tongue, the mystery of the glorious body. Those first three words weren't new.

An older hymn of the cross, by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, opens with the same three. Thomas takes the old opening and turns it from the cross to the altar: the cross and the Eucharist, in one echo.
Then listen to what he does with yesterday's lesson. In the fourth verse: "Verbum caro, panem verum verbo carnem efficit." The Word made flesh, by his word, makes true bread into flesh.

teach.h: WORD AND FLESH IN ONE LINE.
teach.b: Word and flesh, flesh and word, chasing each other across one line: the incarnation and the Eucharist, folded into wordplay a choir can sing.
The same verse goes on: even if the senses fail, faith alone is enough to steady a sincere heart.

teach.h: TANTUM ERGO: SO GREAT A SACRAMENT.
teach.b: And the hymn's last two verses, sung on their own, became the Tantum ergo, the Benediction hymn from day one hundred forty-one: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui."
So great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. A few lines later: "Praestet fides supplementum sensuum defectui."

teach.h: FAITH SUPPLIES WHAT THE SENSES LACK.
teach.b: Let faith supply what the senses lack.

It's yesterday's question about bread that still tastes like bread, answered not in an argument but in a song. The Summa works it out over pages; the hymn hands it to a choir. Same man, same truth, two ways of holding it.

how: Catholics sing the Tantum ergo at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, and the Pange lingua accompanies the procession of the Eucharist at the end of the Holy Thursday Mass and on the feast of Corpus Christi.

practice: If you know the tune of the Tantum ergo, sing the first two lines softly; if not, read them slowly in Latin, one word per breath, Tantum, ergo, Sacramentum, veneremur, cernui, then the English sense: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship.
If you pray, let it be your prayer; if you don't, simply notice what it's like to say an old line slowly.
